claim: Mitochondrial biogenesis requires the import of >1,000 mitochondrial preproteins from the cytosol.
source: Mitochondrial biogenesis requires the import of >1,000 mitochondrial preproteins from the cytosol.
evidence: This is a statement about the number of proteins required for mitochondrial biogenesis, drawing from established scientific knowledge about mitochondrial protein composition.

claim: Pathogenic missense mutations in ANT1 and its yeast homolog Aac2 cause the protein to accumulate along the protein import pathway.
source: Pathogenic missense mutations in ADP/ATP translocase 1 (ANT1), and its yeast homolog ADP/ATP carrier 2 (Aac2), cause the protein to accumulate along the protein import pathway, thereby obstructing general protein translocation into mitochondria.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Mutant ANT1/Aac2 proteins obstruct general protein translocation into mitochondria.
source: Pathogenic missense mutations in ADP/ATP translocase 1 (ANT1), and its yeast homolog ADP/ATP carrier 2 (Aac2), cause the protein to accumulate along the protein import pathway, thereby obstructing general protein translocation into mitochondria.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data showing accumulation of precursor proteins and proteomic evidence.

claim: Protein import clogging by mutant ANT1/Aac2 impairs mitochondrial respiration.
source: This impairs mitochondrial respiration, cytosolic proteostasis, and cell viability independent of ANT1's nucleotide transport activity.
evidence: This is supported by respirometry data presented in the manuscript showing reduced respiratory function in mutant mice.

claim: Protein import clogging by mutant ANT1/Aac2 impairs cytosolic proteostasis.
source: This impairs mitochondrial respiration, cytosolic proteostasis, and cell viability independent of ANT1's nucleotide transport activity.
evidence: This is supported by proteomic data showing accumulation of mitochondrial proteins in the cytosol.

claim: Protein import clogging by mutant ANT1/Aac2 impairs cell viability.
source: This impairs mitochondrial respiration, cytosolic proteostasis, and cell viability independent of ANT1's nucleotide transport activity.
evidence: This is supported by data showing reduced colony formation and cell growth in yeast expressing mutant alleles.

claim: The toxic effects of mutant ANT1/Aac2 are independent of ANT1's nucleotide transport activity.
source: This impairs mitochondrial respiration, cytosolic proteostasis, and cell viability independent of ANT1's nucleotide transport activity.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that catalytically inactive mutants still cause toxicity and that respiration can exceed wild-type levels when complex II is stimulated.

claim: The pathogenic mutations in ANT1/Aac2 act synergistically.
source: The mutations act synergistically, as double mutant Aac2/ANT1 causes severe clogging primarily at the translocase of the outer membrane (TOM) complex.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that double mutants have enhanced toxicity and clogging compared to single mutants.

claim: Double mutant Aac2/ANT1 causes severe clogging primarily at the TOM complex.
source: The mutations act synergistically, as double mutant Aac2/ANT1 causes severe clogging primarily at the translocase of the outer membrane (TOM) complex.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro import assays and co-immunoprecipitation data showing preferential association with TOM complex components.

claim: Double mutant Aac2/ANT1 confers extreme toxicity in yeast.
source: This confers extreme toxicity in yeast.
evidence: This is supported by data showing inability to form colonies and severe growth defects.

claim: Expression of a super-clogger ANT1 variant in mice led to neurodegeneration.
source: In mice, expression of a super-clogger ANT1 variant led to neurodegeneration and an age-dependent dominant myopathy that phenocopy ANT1-induced human disease, suggesting clogging as a mechanism of disease.
evidence: This is supported by histological data showing motor neuron degeneration and GFAP accumulation in the spinal cord.

claim: Expression of a super-clogger ANT1 variant in mice led to an age-dependent dominant myopathy.
source: In mice, expression of a super-clogger ANT1 variant led to neurodegeneration and an age-dependent dominant myopathy that phenocopy ANT1-induced human disease, suggesting clogging as a mechanism of disease.
evidence: This is supported by data showing muscle weakness, myofiber atrophy, and COX-deficient fibers in aged mice.

claim: The phenotypes in mutant ANT1 mice phenocopy ANT1-induced human disease.
source: In mice, expression of a super-clogger ANT1 variant led to neurodegeneration and an age-dependent dominant myopathy that phenocopy ANT1-induced human disease, suggesting clogging as a mechanism of disease.
evidence: This is based on comparison with published clinical features of human ANT1-induced diseases.

claim: Protein import clogging is a mechanism of disease in ANT1-induced human disease.
source: In mice, expression of a super-clogger ANT1 variant led to neurodegeneration and an age-dependent dominant myopathy that phenocopy ANT1-induced human disease, suggesting clogging as a mechanism of disease.
evidence: This is inferred from the mouse model data that recapitulates human disease phenotypes.

claim: There exist uncharacterized amino acid requirements for mitochondrial carrier proteins to avoid clogging and subsequent disease.
source: More broadly, this work implies the existence of uncharacterized amino acid requirements for mitochondrial carrier proteins to avoid clogging and subsequent disease.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion drawn from the findings about specific mutations causing clogging.

claim: The vast majority of mitochondrial proteins are encoded by the nuclear genome.
source: The vast majority of these proteins are encoded by the nuclear genome, synthesized in the cytosol, and sorted into one of the four mitochondrial sub-compartments, namely the outer mitochondrial membrane (OMM), intermembrane space (IMS), inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM), and the matrix (Neupert and Herrmann, 2007; Endo and Yamano, 2009; Chacinska et al., 2009; Wiedemann and Pfanner, 2017).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Nuclear-encoded mitochondrial proteins are synthesized in the cytosol.
source: The vast majority of these proteins are encoded by the nuclear genome, synthesized in the cytosol, and sorted into one of the four mitochondrial sub-compartments, namely the outer mitochondrial membrane (OMM), intermembrane space (IMS), inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM), and the matrix (Neupert and Herrmann, 2007; Endo and Yamano, 2009; Chacinska et al., 2009; Wiedemann and Pfanner, 2017).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Mitochondrial proteins are sorted into one of four mitochondrial sub-compartments: OMM, IMS, IMM, and matrix.
source: The vast majority of these proteins are encoded by the nuclear genome, synthesized in the cytosol, and sorted into one of the four mitochondrial sub-compartments, namely the outer mitochondrial membrane (OMM), intermembrane space (IMS), inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM), and the matrix (Neupert and Herrmann, 2007; Endo and Yamano, 2009; Chacinska et al., 2009; Wiedemann and Pfanner, 2017).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The TOM complex is the entry gate by which >90% of mitochondrial proteins enter mitochondria.
source: The entry gate by which >90% of mitochondrial proteins enter mitochondria is the translocase of the outer membrane (TOM) complex.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about mitochondrial protein import.

claim: Proper function of the TOM complex is paramount for mitochondrial function and cell viability.
source: Therefore, proper function of the TOM complex is paramount for mitochondrial function and cell viability.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the fact that >90% of mitochondrial proteins use the TOM complex.

claim: The import of mitochondrial carrier proteins to the IMM is particularly challenging.
source: The import of mitochondrial carrier proteins to the protein-dense IMM is particularly challenging.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the hydrophobic nature of carrier proteins and the complexity of their import pathway.

claim: Molecular chaperones like Hsp70 and Hsp90 target carrier proteins through the cytosol to the Tom70 receptor.
source: Molecular chaperones like Hsp70 and Hsp90 target these highly hydrophobic proteins through the cytosol to the Tom70 receptor, which is associated with the TOM complex on the mitochondrial surface (Young et al., 2003; Bhangoo et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Tom70 receptor is associated with the TOM complex on the mitochondrial surface.
source: Molecular chaperones like Hsp70 and Hsp90 target these highly hydrophobic proteins through the cytosol to the Tom70 receptor, which is associated with the TOM complex on the mitochondrial surface (Young et al., 2003; Bhangoo et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: After transport through Tom40, the heterohexameric small TIM chaperones transport the preprotein to the TIM22 complex.
source: After transport through the channel-forming Tom40 subunit of the TOM complex, the heterohexameric small TIM chaperones (i.e. the Tim9-Tim10 complex) transport the preprotein to the carrier translocase of the inner membrane (TIM22 complex) (Koehler et al., 1998; Sirrenberg et al., 1998; Wiedemann et al., 2001; Truscott et al., 2002; Webb et al., 2006; Weinhäupl et al., 2018; Ellenrieder et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The carrier translocase inserts carrier proteins into the IMM in a membrane potential-dependent manner.
source: The carrier translocase is a multisubunit complex that inserts carrier proteins into the IMM in a membrane potential (Δψ)-dependent manner (Sirrenberg et al., 1996; Kerscher et al., 1997; Kovermann et al., 2002; Rehling et al., 2003; Zhang et al., 2021; Qi et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Tim22 integrates carrier proteins into the IMM.
source: The central subunit Tim22 integrates carrier proteins into the IMM (Rehling et al., 2003; Peixoto et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In yeast, Tim18 and Sdh3 are required for assembly and stability of the carrier translocase.
source: In yeast, Tim18 and Sdh3 are required for assembly and stability of the carrier translocase, whereas Tim54 tethers the small TIM chaperones (Tim9-Tim10-Tim12 complex) to the translocase (Wagner et al., 2008; Gebert et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In yeast, Tim54 tethers the small TIM chaperones to the translocase.
source: In yeast, Tim18 and Sdh3 are required for assembly and stability of the carrier translocase, whereas Tim54 tethers the small TIM chaperones (Tim9-Tim10-Tim12 complex) to the translocase (Wagner et al., 2008; Gebert et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In human cells, TIM22 associates with AGK and TIM29, which are both required for full import capacity.
source: In human cells, TIM22 associates with the acylglycerol kinase (AGK) and TIM29, which are both required for full import capacity (Kang et al., 2016; Callegari et al., 2016; Kang et al., 2017; Vukotic et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Human TIM22 associates with the TIM9-TIM10 complex.
source: Human TIM22 also associates with the TIM9-TIM10 complex (Qi et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Mutations in TIMM8A have been found in patients suffering Mohr-Tranebjaerg syndrome/deafness dystonia syndrome.
source: For example, mutations in TIMM8A have been found in patients suffering Mohr-Tranebjaerg syndrome/deafness dystonia syndrome (Koehler et al., 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge from published literature supported by citation.

claim: Mutations in TOMM70 and TIMM22 have been linked to a devastating neurological syndrome and a mitochondrial myopathy, respectively.
source: Mutations in TOMM70 and TIMM22 have been linked to a devastating neurological syndrome and a mitochondrial myopathy, respectively (Pacheu-Grau et al., 2018; Dutta et al., 2020; Wei et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge from published literature supported by citations.

claim: Mutations in AGK have been associated with Senger's syndrome marked by cataracts, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, skeletal myopathy, and exercise intolerance.
source: Mutations in another TIM22 complex subunit, AGK, has been associated with the Senger's syndrome marked by cataracts, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, skeletal myopathy, and exercise intolerance (Kang et al., 2017; Vukotic et al., 2017; Mayr et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge from published literature supported by citations.

claim: Defective protein import is linked to neurological and musculoskeletal diseases.
source: Clearly, defective protein import is linked to neurological and musculoskeletal diseases.
evidence: This is inferred from the examples of diseases caused by mutations in protein import machinery components.

claim: Four pathogenic ANT1 variants modeled in yeast Aac2p share numerous dominant phenotypes including cold sensitivity, mtDNA instability, a propensity to misfold inside mitochondria, and hypersensitivity to low Δψ conditions.
source: We previously showed that four pathogenic ANT1 variants modeled in the yeast Aac2p (Figure 1A) share numerous dominant phenotypes including cold sensitivity, mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) instability, a propensity to misfold inside mitochondria, and hypersensitivity to low Δψ conditions (Wang et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2015; Coyne and Chen, 2019).
evidence: This is based on previously published work by the authors, supported by citations.

claim: Transformants expressing aac2M114P,A128P and aac2M114P,A137D formed smaller colonies on selective medium at 25°C relative to wild-type AAC2 and single mutant alleles.
source: We found that transformants expressing aac2M114P,A128P and aac2M114P,A137D formed smaller colonies on the selective medium at 25°C relative to wild-type AAC2 and single mutant alleles (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is directly observed experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Transformants expressing aac2A106D,M114P, aac2A106D,A128P, aac2A106D,A137D, and aac2A128P,A137D were unable to form visible colonies at 25°C.
source: Strikingly, transformants expressing aac2A106D,M114P, aac2A106D,A128P, aac2A106D,A137D, and aac2A128P,A137D were unable to form visible colonies at 25°C.
evidence: This is directly observed experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Growth of transformants expressing some of the double mutants were improved at 30°C.
source: Growth of transformants expressing some of the double mutants were improved at 30°C (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is directly observed experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Combining missense mutations into a single Aac2 protein increases toxicity.
source: These data suggest that combining missense mutations into a single Aac2 protein increases toxicity, even when expressed from a centromeric vector.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing enhanced growth defects in double mutants.

claim: Growth of cells co-expressing aac2A128P,A137D and AAC2 is reduced on glucose medium.
source: We found that growth of cells co-expressing aac2A128P,A137D and AAC2 is reduced on glucose medium (Figure 1C), and they form petites at a much higher frequency compared with those expressing the aac2A128P and aac2A137D single mutant alleles (Figure 1D–E).
evidence: This is directly observed experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Cells co-expressing aac2A128P,A137D and AAC2 form petites at a much higher frequency compared with those expressing single mutant alleles.
source: We found that growth of cells co-expressing aac2A128P,A137D and AAC2 is reduced on glucose medium (Figure 1C), and they form petites at a much higher frequency compared with those expressing the aac2A128P and aac2A137D single mutant alleles (Figure 1D–E).
evidence: This is directly observed experimental data shown in Figures 1D-E.

claim: Neither Aac2pA137D nor Aac2pA128P,A137D supported respiratory growth in the aac2Δ background.
source: In the aac2Δ background, neither Aac2pA137D nor Aac2pA128P,A137D supported respiratory growth (Figure 1C), consistent with the A123D/A137D mutation eliminating nucleotide transport activity (Palmieri et al., 2005).
evidence: This is directly observed experimental data shown in Figure 1C, consistent with published literature.

claim: The A123D/A137D mutation eliminates nucleotide transport activity.
source: In the aac2Δ background, neither Aac2pA137D nor Aac2pA128P,A137D supported respiratory growth (Figure 1C), consistent with the A123D/A137D mutation eliminating nucleotide transport activity (Palmieri et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge from published literature supported by citation.

claim: Cells expressing only aac2A128P,A137D were barely viable.
source: Cells expressing only aac2A128P,A137D were barely viable, and cell growth was completely inhibited at 25°C even on glucose medium (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is directly observed experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Cell growth expressing only aac2A128P,A137D was completely inhibited at 25°C even on glucose medium.
source: Cells expressing only aac2A128P,A137D were barely viable, and cell growth was completely inhibited at 25°C even on glucose medium (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is directly observed experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The severe growth defect of aac2A128P,A137D is in stark contrast to the AAC2-null strain, which strongly supports a dominant effect of aac2A128P,A137D on cell viability.
source: This is in sharp contrast to the AAC2-null strain, which strongly supports a dominant effect of aac2A128P,A137D on cell viability.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the phenotypes of the mutant and null strains.

claim: Aac2pA128P,A137D accumulates to just 4.7% of wild-type Aac2 levels.
source: Interestingly, we found that Aac2pA128P,A137D accumulates to just 4.7% of wild-type Aac2 levels (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: No accumulation of aggregated Aac2pA128P,A137D was observed.
source: We did not observe any accumulation of aggregated Aac2pA128P,A137D (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C), indicating that Aac2pA128P,A137D degradation (see below), rather than aggregation, is the likely explanation for low protein recovery.
evidence: This is directly observed experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C.

claim: Aac2pA128P,A137D degradation, rather than aggregation, is the likely explanation for low protein recovery.
source: We did not observe any accumulation of aggregated Aac2pA128P,A137D (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C), indicating that Aac2pA128P,A137D degradation (see below), rather than aggregation, is the likely explanation for low protein recovery.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of aggregates and subsequent degradation data.

claim: aac2A128P,A137D imparts potent toxicity through a mechanism that is independent of nucleotide transport.
source: Taken together, the data indicate that aac2A128P,A137D imparts potent toxicity through a mechanism that is independent of nucleotide transport.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing toxicity despite lack of respiratory function and low protein levels.

claim: Integration of the double mutant Aac2pA128P,A137D into the IMM was reduced by >70% compared to wild-type.
source: In contrast, integration of the double mutant Aac2pA128P,A137D into the IMM was reduced by >70% (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from in vitro import assays shown in Figures 2A-B.

claim: A significant portion of mutant Aac2p, particularly Aac2pA128P,A137D, is sensitive to proteinase K digestion.
source: We found that a significant portion of mutant Aac2p, particularly Aac2pA128P,A137D, is sensitive to proteinase K digestion (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: This is directly observed experimental data from protease protection assays shown in Figures 2C-D.

claim: Aac2pA128P,A137D had increased association with Tom40-HA compared with wild-type.
source: Indeed, Aac2pA128P,A137D had increased association with Tom40-HA compared with wild-type (Figure 2E–F).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figures 2E-F.

claim: A significant fraction of Aac2pA128P,A137D is arrested at the TOM complex during import into fully energized wild-type mitochondria.
source: These observations suggest that a significant fraction of Aac2pA128P,A137D is arrested at the TOM complex during import into fully energized wild-type mitochondria.
evidence: This is inferred from the protease sensitivity and increased association with Tom40.

claim: Precursor of the mitochondrial matrix protein Hsp60p was readily detectable in cells expressing Aac2pA128P,A137D despite extremely low levels of the mutant protein.
source: Indeed, precursor of the mitochondrial matrix protein Hsp60p was readily detectable in cells expressing Aac2pA128P,A137D despite extremely low levels of the mutant protein (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is directly observed experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The timing of Hsp60p precursor accumulation was coupled with the induction of the mutant Aac2p.
source: Importantly, the timing of Hsp60p precursor accumulation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) was coupled with the induction of the mutant Aac2p (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is directly observed experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-C.

claim: The mutant Aac2p directly affects the import of other mitochondrial proteins in vivo.
source: The data suggest that the mutant Aac2p directly affects the import of other mitochondrial proteins in vivo.
evidence: This is inferred from the temporal correlation between mutant protein induction and precursor accumulation.

claim: In transformants expressing double mutant aac2 alleles from a centromeric vector, the level of un-cleaved Hsp60p correlated with toxicity.
source: In transformants expressing double mutant aac2 alleles from a centromeric vector, the level of un-cleaved Hsp60p correlated with toxicity (Figure 2H, see also Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is observed from comparing data across multiple figures showing both Hsp60p levels and growth phenotypes.

claim: Total Aac2p levels were reduced by all double mutant Aac2p variants except the least toxic Aac2pM114P,A137D.
source: Moreover, total Aac2p levels were reduced by all double mutant Aac2p variants except the least toxic Aac2pM114P,A137D (Figure 2H–I).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figures 2H-I.

claim: The extent of endogenous Aac2 reduction correlated with cell toxicity.
source: The extent of endogenous Aac2 reduction also correlated with cell toxicity.
evidence: This is observed from comparing protein levels with growth phenotypes across different mutants.

claim: MG132 failed to increase the steady-state level of Aac2pA128P,A137D.
source: Interestingly, we found that MG132 failed to increase the steady-state level of Aac2pA128P,A137D (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is directly observed experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Proteasome dysfunction induced by ump1Δ and pre9Δ did not increase Aac2pA128P,A137D levels.
source: As an orthogonal approach, we tested whether proteasome dysfunction induced by two temperature-sensitive mutants, ump1Δ and pre9Δ, could increase Aac2pA128P,A137D levels, and observed no effect (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: This is directly observed experimental data shown in Figures 3B-C.

claim: The mutant protein Aac2pA128P,A137D is unstable compared with the wild-type Aac2p.
source: Cyclohexamide chase following a galactose-induced Aac2pA128P,A137D synthesis confirmed that the mutant protein is unstable compared with the wild-type Aac2p (Figure 3D–E).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from cycloheximide chase experiments shown in Figures 3D-E.

claim: MG132 failed to stabilize acutely induced Aac2pA128P,A137D.
source: Consistently, MG132 failed to stabilize acutely induced Aac2pA128P,A137D.
evidence: This is directly observed experimental data from cycloheximide chase experiments with MG132 treatment.

claim: Little, if any, Aac2pA128P,A137D is degraded by the proteasome.
source: These data suggest that little, if any, Aac2pA128P,A137D is degraded by the proteasome.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of effect of proteasome inhibition on protein levels.

claim: Aac2pA128P,A137D is significantly but not fully stabilized in cells disrupted of YME1.
source: Indeed, we found that Aac2pA128P,A137D is significantly but not fully stabilized in cells disrupted of YME1 (Figure 3D–E).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from cycloheximide chase experiments in yme1Δ cells shown in Figures 3D-E.

claim: Inhibition of proteasomal function with MG132 does not significantly stabilize Aac2pA128P,A137D in yme1Δ cells.
source: Inhibition of proteasomal function with MG132 does not significantly stabilize Aac2pA128P,A137D in yme1Δ cells.
evidence: This is directly observed experimental data from cycloheximide chase experiments.

claim: Yme1p plays an important role in the degradation of Aac2pA128P,A137D.
source: These data strongly suggest that Yme1p plays an important role in the degradation of Aac2pA128P,A137D, possibly serving as a quality control mechanism for degrading stalled import substrates in the vicinity of TIM22 and/or the TOM complex (Wu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is inferred from the stabilization of the mutant protein in yme1Δ cells.

claim: Yme1p possibly serves as a quality control mechanism for degrading stalled import substrates in the vicinity of TIM22 and/or the TOM complex.
source: These data strongly suggest that Yme1p plays an important role in the degradation of Aac2pA128P,A137D, possibly serving as a quality control mechanism for degrading stalled import substrates in the vicinity of TIM22 and/or the TOM complex (Wu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is speculative interpretation of the data, supported by a citation.

claim: Numerous proteins preferentially co-purify with Aac2pA128P-HIS6 over Aac2p-HIS6.
source: Numerous proteins preferentially co-purify with Aac2pA128P-HIS6 over Aac2p-HIS6 (Figure 4—source data 1), which were enriched for chaperones involved in targeting of mitochondrial preproteins through the cytosol (Figure 4C; Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from quantitative proteomics shown in Figure 4C and supplementary figures.

claim: Proteins that preferentially co-purify with Aac2pA128P-HIS6 were enriched for chaperones involved in targeting of mitochondrial preproteins through the cytosol.
source: Numerous proteins preferentially co-purify with Aac2pA128P-HIS6 over Aac2p-HIS6 (Figure 4—source data 1), which were enriched for chaperones involved in targeting of mitochondrial preproteins through the cytosol (Figure 4C; Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: This is based on enrichment analysis of proteomic data shown in Figure 4C and supplementary figures.

claim: Aac2pA128P has increased association with the TOM complex.
source: Aac2pA128P also has increased association with the TOM complex, as well as the translocase of the inner membrane (TIM22) complex that is responsible for the Δψ-dependent insertion of carrier proteins into the IMM (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from quantitative proteomics shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Aac2pA128P has increased association with the TIM22 complex.
source: Aac2pA128P also has increased association with the TOM complex, as well as the translocase of the inner membrane (TIM22) complex that is responsible for the Δψ-dependent insertion of carrier proteins into the IMM (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from quantitative proteomics shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The association of Aac2pA128P with Tim22p was confirmed by immunoblotting.
source: The association with Tim22p was confirmed by immunoblotting (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G–H).
evidence: This is directly observed experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G–H.

claim: There is no increased association of Aac2pA128P with Tim23p.
source: Expectedly, there is no increased association of Aac2pA128P with Tim23p, which is known to associate with wild-type Aac2p and is not involved in its import (Figure 4—figure supplement 1I; Dienhart and Stuart, 2008).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1I, consistent with published literature.

claim: Tim23p is known to associate with wild-type Aac2p and is not involved in its import.
source: Expectedly, there is no increased association of Aac2pA128P with Tim23p, which is known to associate with wild-type Aac2p and is not involved in its import (Figure 4—figure supplement 1I; Dienhart and Stuart, 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge from published literature supported by citation.

claim: Approximately 5 mmoles of Tim22p are pulled down per mole of Aac2pA128P-HIS6.
source: We found that ~5 mmoles of Tim22p are pulled down per mole of Aac2pA128P-HIS6 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from targeted quantitative proteomics shown in Figure 4D.

claim: If 5 mmoles per mole of Aac2pA128P molecules are bound to Tim22p in vivo, this could theoretically occupy ~85% of Tim22p channels.
source: If 5 mmoles per mole of Aac2pA128P molecules are bound to Tim22p in vivo, this could theoretically occupy ~85% of Tim22p channels, as Aac2p is present at ~188,000 molecules per cell and Tim22p at just 1100 (Morgenstern et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a calculation based on measured stoichiometry and published protein abundance data.

claim: Aac2p is present at ~188,000 molecules per cell and Tim22p at just 1100.
source: If 5 mmoles per mole of Aac2pA128P molecules are bound to Tim22p in vivo, this could theoretically occupy ~85% of Tim22p channels, as Aac2p is present at ~188,000 molecules per cell and Tim22p at just 1100 (Morgenstern et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge from published literature supported by citation.

claim: Aac2pA128P is stalled at both the TOM and TIM22 complexes during import.
source: Taken together, the data suggest that Aac2pA128P is stalled at both the TOM and TIM22 complexes during import.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-immunoprecipitation and proteomic data showing association with both complexes.

claim: aac2A128P-expressing cells are sensitive to genetic perturbation to the carrier import pathway.
source: First, we observed that aac2A128P-expressing cells are sensitive to genetic perturbation to the carrier import pathway.
evidence: This is directly observed from genetic interaction experiments.

claim: Meiotic segregants combining aac2A128P expression with tom70Δ or tim18Δ form barely visible microcolonies at 30°C on glucose medium.
source: We found that meiotic segregants combining aac2A128P expression with tom70Δ or tim18Δ form barely visible microcolonies at 30°C on glucose medium (Figure 4E–F).
evidence: This is directly observed experimental data shown in Figures 4E-F.

claim: Tom70p's primary function is to recruit chaperones to the mitochondrial surface to prevent proteotoxicity in this protein-dense region.
source: It was recently proposed that Tom70p's primary function is to recruit chaperones to the mitochondrial surface to prevent proteotoxicity in this protein-dense region (Backes et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge from recently published literature supported by citation.

claim: CIS1 transcript levels are acutely increased upon expression of aac2A128P, but not of AAC2, from a GAL10 promoter.
source: We found that CIS1 transcript levels are acutely increased upon expression of aac2A128P, but not of AAC2, from a GAL10 promoter (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from qRT-PCR shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3B.

claim: CIS1 upregulation is the hallmark of the mitochondrial compromised protein import response (mitoCPR).
source: CIS1 upregulation is the hallmark of the mitochondrial compromised protein import response (mitoCPR) (Weidberg and Amon, 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge from published literature supported by citation.

claim: RPN4, HSP82, SSA3, and SSA4 are transiently upregulated upon aac2A128P expression.
source: We also found that RPN4, HSP82, SSA3, and SSA4 are transiently upregulated (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C–F), consistent with previously published gene activation patterns induced by a synthetic mitochondrial protein import clogger (Boos et al., 2019).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from qRT-PCR shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3C–F.

claim: The transcriptional response to aac2A128P expression is consistent with previously published gene activation patterns induced by a synthetic mitochondrial protein import clogger.
source: We also found that RPN4, HSP82, SSA3, and SSA4 are transiently upregulated (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C–F), consistent with previously published gene activation patterns induced by a synthetic mitochondrial protein import clogger (Boos et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on comparison with published literature supported by citation.

claim: aac2A128P,A137D expression renders cells hypersensitive to defects in phospholipid homeostasis.
source: Interestingly, we found that aac2A128P,A137D expression renders cells hypersensitive to defects in phospholipid homeostasis.
evidence: This is directly observed from genetic interaction experiments with pel1Δ and psd1Δ.

claim: Expression of aac2A128P,A137D strongly inhibited the growth of cells in pel1Δ and psd1Δ genetic backgrounds.
source: We expressed aac2A128P,A137D in cells impaired in production of cardiolipin (CL) (pel1Δ) and phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) (psd1Δ). Expression of aac2A128P,A137D strongly inhibited the growth of cells in these genetic backgrounds (Figure 4—figure supplement 3G–H).
evidence: This is directly observed experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3G–H.

claim: CL and PE facilitate mitochondrial protein import.
source: The data are consistent with previous observations that CL and PE facilitate mitochondrial protein import (Becker et al., 2013; Gebert et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge from published literature supported by citations.

claim: Combining missense mutations in Ant1 dramatically reduced steady-state protein levels in human cells.
source: Like in yeast, combining missense mutations in Ant1 dramatically reduced steady-state protein levels, suggesting impaired ANT1 biogenesis (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The level of ANT1A114P,A123D is only 2.2% of the wild-type in human cells.
source: Most strikingly, the level of ANT1A114P,A123D, equivalent to the yeast Aac2pA128P,A137D, is only 2.2% of the wild-type.
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from immunoblotting.

claim: ANT1A114P has increased interactions with components of both TOM and TIM22 complexes in human cells.
source: First, immunoprecipitation of ANT1A114P-HA demonstrated that the mutant protein has increased interactions with components of both TOM and TIM22 complexes (Figure 5B–C), as observed with its yeast ortholog Aac2pA128P.
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from co-immunoprecipitation shown in Figures 5B-C.

claim: 42% and 52% of total ANT1A114P and ANT1A114P,A123D proteins are exposed on the OMM, whereas the wild-type ANT1 is protected from proteinase K digestion.
source: Second, protease protection assay demonstrated that 42% and 52% of total ANT1A114P and ANT1A114P,A123D proteins are exposed on the OMM, whereas the wild-type ANT1 is protected from proteinase K digestion (Figure 5D–E).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from protease protection assays shown in Figures 5D-E.

claim: Mitochondrial proteins accumulate in the cytosol of SLC25A4 p.A114P and SLC25A4 p.A114P,A123D-transfected cells, compared with wild-type Ant1-transfected cells.
source: Third, proteomics demonstrated that mitochondrial proteins accumulate in the cytosol of SLC25A4 p.A114P and SLC25A4 p.A114P,A123D -transfected cells, compared with wild-type Ant1-transfected cells (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from quantitative proteomics shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Mitochondrial matrix proteins were significantly enriched in the cytosol of ANT1A114P,A123D versus ANT1-expressing cells.
source: Moreover, mitochondrial matrix proteins were significantly enriched in the cytosol of ANT1A114P,A123D versus ANT1-expressing cells (FDR<3×10–6) (Figure 5G; Figure 5—source data 1), corroborating that the double mutant Aac2p impairs global protein import.
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from quantitative proteomics with statistical analysis shown in Figure 5G.

claim: ANT1A114P and ANT1A114P,A123D clog protein import in human cells, with ANT1A114P,A123D having enhanced clogging activity despite low protein levels.
source: We therefore conclude that ANT1A114P and ANT1A114P,A123D clog protein import in human cells, with ANT1A114P,A123D having enhanced clogging activity despite low protein levels.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of experimental evidence in human cells.

claim: Neither ANT1A114P,A123D nor its single mutant counterparts reduced Δψ or significantly increased cell death compared with wild-type.
source: However, neither ANT1A114P,A123D nor its single mutant counterparts reduced Δψ or significantly increased cell death compared with wild-type (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from flow cytometry shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The effect on protein import by ANT1A114P and ANT1A114P,A123D is likely due to their physical retention in the import pathway rather than due to reduction of Δψ.
source: Thus, the effect on protein import by ANT1A114P and ANT1A114P,A123D is likely due to their physical retention in the import pathway rather than due to reduction of Δψ.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of effect on membrane potential.

claim: A neurodegeneration phenotype that culminates in paralysis occurred in some Slc25a4 p.A114P,A123D/+ mice.
source: We observed a neurodegeneration phenotype that culminates in paralysis in some Slc25a4 p.A114P,A123D/+ mice (Figure 6C; Video 1; Video 2).
evidence: This is directly observed phenotype documented in Figure 6C and videos.

claim: The neurodegeneration phenotype occurred in only four Slc25a4 p.A114P,A123D/+ mice, with a penetrance of 3.4% among the heterozygous mice that have reached 15 months of age.
source: This phenotype occurred in only four Slc25a4 p.A114P,A123D/+ mice, with a penetrance of 3.4% among the heterozygous mice that have reached 15 months of age.
evidence: This is directly observed and calculated from the mouse colony data.

claim: The presenting symptom of neurodegeneration in Slc25a4 p.A114P,A123D/+ mice is typically altered gait after the age of 11 months, followed by weight loss and death within 2–3 weeks of symptom onset.
source: The presenting symptom is typically altered gait after the age of 11 months, followed by weight loss and death within 2–3 weeks of symptom onset.
evidence: This is directly observed from monitoring the affected mice.

claim: Histological analysis of the lumbar spinal cord in a symptomatic Slc25a4 p.A114P,A123D/+ mouse demonstrated dissolution of Nissl substance in the cell bodies of ventral horn neurons.
source: Histological analysis of the lumbar spinal cord in a symptomatic Slc25a4 p.A114P,A123D/+ mouse demonstrated dissolution of Nissl substance in the cell bodies of ventral horn neurons (Figure 6D), consistent with motor neuron degeneration (Bodian and Mellors, 1945).
evidence: This is directly observed histological data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Dissolution of Nissl substance in ventral horn neurons is consistent with motor neuron degeneration.
source: Histological analysis of the lumbar spinal cord in a symptomatic Slc25a4 p.A114P,A123D/+ mouse demonstrated dissolution of Nissl substance in the cell bodies of ventral horn neurons (Figure 6D), consistent with motor neuron degeneration (Bodian and Mellors, 1945).
evidence: This is established knowledge from published literature supported by citation.

claim: Neurodegeneration in the spinal cord of Slc25a4 p.A114P,A123D/+ mice was indicated by GFAP accumulation.
source: Neurodegeneration in the spinal cord was also indicated by GFAP accumulation by immunofluorescence and immunoblotting (Figure 6E–G).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figures 6E-G.

claim: Transmission electron microscopy of ventral horn neurons in Slc25a4 p.A114P,A123D/+ mice revealed loss of cristae density of mitochondria.
source: Transmission electron microscopy of ventral horn neurons revealed loss of cristae density of mitochondria, which suggests defects in mitochondrial biogenesis (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is directly observed ultrastructural data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: Loss of cristae density in mitochondria suggests defects in mitochondrial biogenesis.
source: Transmission electron microscopy of ventral horn neurons revealed loss of cristae density of mitochondria, which suggests defects in mitochondrial biogenesis (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is inferred from the ultrastructural observations.

claim: The maximal respiratory rate (state 3) of Slc25a4 p.A114P,A123D/+ muscle mitochondria was reduced by ~20% and ~30% when utilizing complex I in 9- and 24-month-old mice, respectively.
source: Consistent with clinical phenotypes, we found that the maximal respiratory rate (state 3) of Slc25a4 p.A114P,A123D/+ muscle mitochondria was reduced by ~20% and ~30% when utilizing complex I in 9- and 24-month-old mice, respectively (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from respirometry shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The respiratory control ratio was reduced by ~31% and ~42% in young and old Slc25a4 p.A114P,A123D/+ mice, respectively.
source: The respiratory control ratio, which is the single most useful and sensitive general measure of energy coupling efficiency (Brand and Nicholls, 2011), was reduced by ~31% and ~42% in young and old mice, respectively.
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from respirometry.

claim: The respiratory control ratio is the single most useful and sensitive general measure of energy coupling efficiency.
source: The respiratory control ratio, which is the single most useful and sensitive general measure of energy coupling efficiency (Brand and Nicholls, 2011), was reduced by ~31% and ~42% in young and old mice, respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge from published literature supported by citation.

claim: When complex I is inhibited and complex II substrate (succinate) is present, maximal respiration is increased by ~23% in the Slc25a4 p.A114P,A123D/+ mutant mice at 9 months of age.
source: Surprisingly, when complex I is inhibited and complex II substrate (succinate) is present, maximal respiration is increased by ~23% in the mutant mice at 9 months of age (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from respirometry shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The increased respiration with complex II substrate confirms that ATP/ADP transport is not a limiting factor for sustaining a high respiratory rate in Slc25a4 p.A114P,A123D/+ mice.
source: This result is important because it confirms that ATP/ADP transport is not a limiting factor for sustaining a high respiratory rate in Slc25a4 p.A114P,A123D/+ mice.
evidence: This is inferred from the respirometry data showing increased respiration with complex II substrate.

claim: Slc25a4 knockout displays a >30% reduction in complex II-based respiration.
source: This is in stark contrast to Slc25a4 knockout, which displays a >30% reduction in complex II-based respiration (Graham et al., 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge from published literature supported by citation.

claim: Slc25a4 p.A114P,A123D/+ mice exhibit significant reduction in myofiber diameter.
source: In addition to mild bioenergetic defect, we detected significant reduction in myofiber diameter in the skeletal muscle from aged Slc25a4 p.A114P,A123D/+ mice (Figure 7C–D).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from histological analysis shown in Figures 7C-D.

claim: Approximately 3.5% of myofibers in aged Slc25a4 p.A114P,A123D/+ mice have reduced COX and SDH activity centrally, but remained COX and SDH-positive in the periphery.
source: Instead, we found that ~3.5% of myofibers have reduced COX and SDH activity centrally, but remained COX and SDH-positive in the periphery (Figure 7E–G).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from histochemical analysis shown in Figures 7E-G.

claim: Slc25a4 p.A114P,A123D/+ mice display muscle weakness.
source: Finally, we found that the Slc25a4 p.A114P,A123D/+ mice display muscle weakness (Figure 7H–I).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from grip strength testing shown in Figures 7H-I.

claim: Slc25a4 p.A114P,A123D induces a dominant myopathic phenotype.
source: These data demonstrate that Slc25a4 p.A114P,A123D induces a dominant myopathic phenotype.
evidence: This is concluded from the multiple lines of evidence showing muscle pathology in heterozygous mice.

claim: The Ant1A114P,A123D protein is virtually undetectable in the total lysates of mouse tissues.
source: We found that the Ant1A114P,A123D protein is virtually undetectable in the total lysates of mouse tissues, suggesting a rapid degradation of the mutant protein as observed in yeast and human cells. (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is directly observed experimental data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Ant1A114P,A123D was present at ~0.1% of wild-type level in isolated skeletal muscle mitochondria.
source: Only in isolated skeletal muscle mitochondria were we able to detect Ant1A114P,A123D, which was present at ~0.1% of wild-type level (Figure 8B–C).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figures 8B-C.

claim: Ant1A114P,A123D is more sensitive to proteinase K digestion compared with wild-type Ant1 in isolated muscle mitochondria.
source: Protease protection assay on isolated muscle mitochondria demonstrated that Ant1A114P,A123D is more sensitive to proteinase K digestion compared with wild-type Ant1 (Figure 8D–E), consistent with import clogging in vivo.
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from protease protection assays shown in Figures 8D-E.

claim: Smac appears to be more sensitive to proteinase K in Slc25a4 p.A114P,A123D/Slc25a4 p.A114P,A123D mitochondria.
source: Moreover, Smac also appears to be more sensitive to proteinase K in Slc25a4 p.A114P,A123D/Slc25a4 p.A114P,A123D mitochondria, while Mdh2 and Tim23 do not (Figure 8F–H).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from protease protection assays shown in Figures 8F-H.

claim: Clogging does not affect all mitochondrial preproteins equally.
source: While this could indicate instability or partial rupture of the OMM in mutant mitochondria, it could also be a result of clogging and imply that clogging does not affect all mitochondrial preproteins equally.
evidence: This is speculative interpretation of the differential protease sensitivity data.

claim: The Tom40 β-barrel pore contains several distinct protein paths.
source: This could be explained by the observation that the Tom40 β-barrel pore contains several distinct protein paths (Shiota et al., 2015; Araiso et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge from published literature supported by citations.

claim: There is a striking global increase in mitochondrial proteins in the cytosol of Slc25a4 p.A114P,A123D/+ muscle.
source: We found a striking global increase in mitochondrial proteins in the cytosol of Slc25a4 p.A114P,A123D/+ muscle (Figure 8J).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from quantitative proteomics shown in Figure 8J.

claim: Among the 75 proteins increased by at least 25% in the cytosol (p<0.05), proteins assigned to the mitochondrion accounted for 45 of them.
source: Among the 75 proteins increased by at least 25% in the cytosol (p<0.05), proteins assigned to the mitochondrion accounted for 45 of them (Figure 8—source data 1).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from quantitative proteomics analysis.

claim: The enrichment of mitochondrial proteins in the cytosol of Slc25a4 p.A114P,A123D/+ muscle was highly significant (FDR<10–33).
source: This enrichment was highly significant (FDR<10–33).
evidence: This is the statistical analysis result from the proteomic data.

claim: Ant1A114P,A123D clogs general protein import in vivo.
source: Taken together, the data suggest that Ant1A114P,A123D clogs general protein import in vivo.
evidence: This is concluded from the proteomic evidence of mitochondrial protein accumulation in the cytosol.

claim: There is a trend of increase in proteasomal subunits and Hsp70 proteins in the cytosol of Slc25a4 p.A114P,A123D/+ muscle.
source: Supporting this is a trend of increase in proteasomal subunits and Hsp70 proteins in the cytosol of Slc25a4 p.A114P,A123D/+muscle, which suggests an anti-mPOS response (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is observed from the proteomic data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: The respiratory complexes and supercomplexes were minimally affected in Slc25a4 p.A114P,A123D/+ muscle mitochondria.
source: The respiratory complexes and supercomplexes were minimally affected (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C–D), as was the TIM23 complex (Figure 8—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is directly observed experimental data from BN-PAGE shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C–E.

claim: The TIM23 complex was minimally affected in Slc25a4 p.A114P,A123D/+ muscle mitochondria.
source: The respiratory complexes and supercomplexes were minimally affected (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C–D), as was the TIM23 complex (Figure 8—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is directly observed experimental data from BN-PAGE shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1E.

claim: There were minimal changes in the steady-state levels of mitochondrial proteins in Slc25a4 p.A114P,A123D/+ muscle mitochondria.
source: We found minimal changes in the steady-state levels of mitochondrial proteins, including other Ant isoforms (Figure 8—figure supplement 1F, Figure 8—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from quantitative proteomics shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1F.

claim: A focused analysis on mitochondrial proteases and chaperones suggested a subtle but statistically significant increase in the mitochondrial proteostatic machinery.
source: Interestingly, a focused analysis on mitochondrial proteases and chaperones suggested a subtle but statistically significant increase in the mitochondrial proteostatic machinery (p=2.7 × 10–14, analyzed with a two-way ANOVA; Figure 8—figure supplement 1G), which supports proteostatic stress inside mitochondria.
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from quantitative proteomics with statistical analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Mitochondrial proteomics suggested global increase in TIM22 pathway components in Slc25a4 p.A114P,A123D/+ muscle.
source: Our mitochondrial proteomics dataset suggested global increase in TIM22 pathway components (Figure 8—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from quantitative proteomics shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Tim22 levels showed an ~40% increase in Slc25a4 p.A114P,A123D/+ muscle mitochondria.
source: Immunoblot validation of Tim22 showed an ~40% increase (Figure 8—figure supplement 1I–J).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from immunoblotting shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1I–J.

claim: The increase in TIM22 pathway components may represent chronic adaptation to carrier protein import clogging.
source: These data may represent chronic adaptation to carrier protein import clogging, though more work is required to rigorously test this hypothesis.
evidence: This is speculative interpretation of the proteomic data.

claim: eIF2α phosphorylation was not increased in Slc25a4 p.A114P,A123D/+ mouse skeletal muscle at multiple ages.
source: First, eIF2α phosphorylation, a hallmark of the ISR, was not increased in Slc25a4 p.A114P,A123D/+ mouse skeletal muscle at multiple ages (Figure 8—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from immunoblotting shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2A–B.

claim: Transcriptomic analysis in Slc25a4 p.A114P,A123D/+ skeletal muscle failed to show induction of ISR target genes.
source: Second, transcriptomic analysis in Slc25a4 p.A114P,A123D/+ skeletal muscle failed to show induction of ISR target genes (Figure 8—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from RNA-seq shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Transcription factor enrichment analysis of significantly upregulated genes revealed activation of pathways controlled by FOXO1 and FOXO3.
source: Instead, transcription factor enrichment analysis of significantly upregulated genes (q<0.05) revealed activation of pathways controlled by novel transcriptional factors, including FOXO1 and FOXO3 that are involved in metabolic homeostasis and autophagy (Figure 8—figure supplement 2D–E).
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2D–E.

claim: FOXO1 and FOXO3 are involved in metabolic homeostasis and autophagy.
source: Instead, transcription factor enrichment analysis of significantly upregulated genes (q<0.05) revealed activation of pathways controlled by novel transcriptional factors, including FOXO1 and FOXO3 that are involved in metabolic homeostasis and autophagy (Figure 8—figure supplement 2D–E).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the functions of these transcription factors.

claim: Slc25a4 p.A114P,A123D induces an entirely unique transcriptional signature.
source: It appeared that Slc25a4 p.A114P,A123D induces an entirely unique transcriptional signature (Figure 8—figure supplement 2F; Figure 8—figure supplement 2—source data 1), although it remains to be determined whether severe mitochondrial protein import clogging relative to Ant1A114P,A123D induces similar stress responses and/or activates ISR.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2F.

claim: Depp1 is known to activate autophagy.
source: Among the upregulated genes, Depp1 is known to activate autophagy (Stepp et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge from published literature supported by citation.

claim: There is very limited overlap in the enrichment profile among significantly altered genes when comparing Slc25a4 p.A114P,A123D/+ to Slc25a4 knockout mice.
source: More importantly, when directly compared to Slc25a4 knockout mice (Morrow et al., 2017), there is very limited overlap in the enrichment profile among significantly altered genes (Figure 8—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: This is based on comparative analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2G.

claim: The primary stress in Slc25a4 p.A114P,A123D/+ skeletal muscle is distinct from that in Ant1 knockout mice.
source: This indicates that the primary stress in Slc25a4 p.A114P,A123D/+ skeletal muscle is distinct from that in Ant1 knockout mice.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of overlap in transcriptional signatures.

claim: Ant1A114P,A123D dominantly causes muscle and low-penetrant neurological disease in mice that recapitulates pathological and molecular phenotypes of dominant Ant1-induced diseases in humans.
source: In summary, we found that Ant1A114P,A123D dominantly causes muscle and low-penetrant neurological disease in mice that recapitulates pathological and molecular phenotypes of dominant Ant1-induced diseases in humans.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the mouse phenotyping data.

claim: The mouse model data corroborates the toxicity of Aac2A128P,A137D in yeast.
source: This corroborates the toxicity of Aac2A128P,A137D in yeast (Figure 1), and supports the idea that mitochondrial protein import clogging by a mutant substrate preprotein is pathogenic.
evidence: This is inferred from the consistency of findings across yeast and mouse models.

claim: Mitochondrial protein import clogging by a mutant substrate preprotein is pathogenic.
source: This corroborates the toxicity of Aac2A128P,A137D in yeast (Figure 1), and supports the idea that mitochondrial protein import clogging by a mutant substrate preprotein is pathogenic.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study supported by data from multiple model systems.

claim: Failure in mitochondrial protein import has severe physiological consequences.
source: Failure in mitochondrial protein import has severe physiological consequences.
evidence: This is established knowledge and also supported by the findings of this study.

claim: Failure in mitochondrial protein import causes toxic accumulation and aggregation of mitochondrial preproteins in the cytosol, a process termed mitochondrial Precursor Overaccumulation Stress (mPOS).
source: In addition to defective mitochondrial biogenesis and energy metabolism, it also causes toxic accumulation and aggregation of mitochondrial preproteins in the cytosol, a process termed mitochondrial Precursor Overaccumulation Stress (mPOS) (Wang and Chen, 2015; Coyne and Chen, 2018; Song et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge from published literature supported by citations.

claim: Many cellular safeguards have been identified that can maintain protein import efficiency and/or mitigate mPOS.
source: To prevent these consequences, many cellular safeguards have been identified that can maintain protein import efficiency and/or mitigate mPOS (Backes et al., 2021; Weidberg and Amon, 2018; Boos et al., 2019; Izawa et al., 2012; Wrobel et al., 2015; Nargund et al., 2015; Izawa et al., 2017; Hansen et al., 2018; Zurita Rendón et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2019; Mårtensson et al., 2019; Su et al., 2019; Ordureau et al., 2020; Phu et al., 2020; Xiao et al., 2021; Shakya et al., 2021; Xin et al., 2022; Sam et al., 2021; Schulte et al., 2023; Dewar et al., 2022; Krämer et al., 2023).
evidence: This is established knowledge from published literature supported by multiple citations.

claim: Studies on mitochondrial stressors that impair protein import have been mainly focused on mutations that directly affect the core protein import machinery, synthetic clogger proteins, or on pharmacological interventions that reduce Δψ.
source: So far, studies on mitochondrial stressors that impair protein import have been mainly focused on mutations that directly affect the core protein import machinery, synthetic clogger proteins, or on pharmacological interventions that reduce Δψ (Song et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a summary of the state of the field supported by citation.

claim: This report uncovered the first example of naturally occurring missense mutations in an endogenous mitochondrial protein causing toxic protein import clogging.
source: In this report, we have uncovered the first example of naturally occurring missense mutations in an endogenous mitochondrial protein causing toxic protein import clogging.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings.

claim: A single protein without overexpression is sufficient to clog import.
source: We showed that a single protein without overexpression is sufficient to clog import, thereby inducing robust protein import stress responses, bioenergetic defects, and cytosolic proteostatic stress.
evidence: This is a key finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Protein import clogging induces robust protein import stress responses, bioenergetic defects, and cytosolic proteostatic stress.
source: We showed that a single protein without overexpression is sufficient to clog import, thereby inducing robust protein import stress responses, bioenergetic defects, and cytosolic proteostatic stress.
evidence: This is supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence including transcriptional analysis, respirometry, and proteomics.

claim: Import clogging kills yeast cells.
source: The data supports a model in which import clogging kills yeast cells and contributes to muscle and neurological degeneration in mice.
evidence: This is supported by the growth defects and lethality observed in yeast expressing mutant alleles.

claim: Import clogging contributes to muscle and neurological degeneration in mice.
source: The data supports a model in which import clogging kills yeast cells and contributes to muscle and neurological degeneration in mice.
evidence: This is supported by the phenotypes observed in the mouse model.

claim: The mitochondrial carrier protein family is the largest of the transporter families.
source: The mitochondrial carrier protein family is the largest of the transporter families and has highly conserved domain and sequence features across all eukaryotes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mitochondrial carrier proteins.

claim: Mitochondrial carrier proteins have highly conserved domain and sequence features across all eukaryotes.
source: The mitochondrial carrier protein family is the largest of the transporter families and has highly conserved domain and sequence features across all eukaryotes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mitochondrial carrier proteins.

claim: Carrier proteins assume partially folded conformations called 'hairpin loops' that place adjacent hydrophobic α-helices antiparallel with one another during import.
source: Their import into mitochondria is unique in that they assume partially folded conformations called 'hairpin loops' that place adjacent hydrophobic α-helices antiparallel with one another (de Marcos-Lousa et al., 2006; Wiedemann et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge from published literature supported by citations.

claim: There are three 'hairpin loop' modules per carrier preprotein that transit through the Tom40 β-barrel in a loop-first topology.
source: There are three 'hairpin loop' modules per carrier preprotein that transit through the Tom40 β-barrel in a loop-first topology, such that the C- and N-termini initially remain exposed to the cytosol.
evidence: This is established knowledge about carrier protein import mechanism.

claim: The Tom40 β-barrel can only accommodate the width of up to two α-helical segments at a time.
source: This leaves little wiggle room for the carrier preprotein considering the Tom40 β-barrel can only accommodate the width of up to two α-helical segments at a time (Wiedemann et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge from published literature supported by citation.

claim: The hydrophobic hairpin loops are thought to be guided by an array of hydrophobic patches on the inside of the Tom40 pore.
source: To get through the Tom40 β-barrel pore, the hydrophobic hairpin loops are thought to be guided by an array of hydrophobic patches on the inside of the pore (Shiota et al., 2015; Araiso et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge from published literature supported by citations.

claim: Dominant pathogenic mutations in ANT1 are found in the hydrophobic α-helices.
source: It is in the hydrophobic α-helices of the ADP/ATP translocase ANT1 (Aac2p in yeast) that dominant pathogenic mutations are found, which introduce either a proline or an aspartic acid (see Figure 1).
evidence: This is based on the location of mutations shown in Figure 1.

claim: Pathogenic mutations in ANT1 introduce either a proline or an aspartic acid into hydrophobic α-helices.
source: It is in the hydrophobic α-helices of the ADP/ATP translocase ANT1 (Aac2p in yeast) that dominant pathogenic mutations are found, which introduce either a proline or an aspartic acid (see Figure 1).
evidence: This is based on the nature of the mutations shown in Figure 1.

claim: Pathogenic mutations in ANT1/Aac2 cause the protein to arrest at or in the TOM complex.
source: Here, we show that these mutations cause the protein to arrest at or in the TOM complex, thereby partially obstructing general protein import.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by in vitro import assays and co-immunoprecipitation data.

claim: Carrier preproteins appear to form partial α-helical secondary structures while bound to the Tim9-Tim10 chaperone.
source: Interestingly, carrier preproteins appear to form partial α-helical secondary structures while bound to the Tim9-Tim10 chaperone (Weinhäupl et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge from published literature supported by citation.

claim: One of the most surprising observations of this study was the extreme toxicity of the double mutant clogger proteins that arrest at the TOM complex.
source: One of the most surprising observations of this study was the extreme toxicity of the double mutant clogger proteins that arrest at the TOM complex.
evidence: This is a reflection on the significance of the findings.

claim: The deleterious stressors downstream of clogging are likely to be multifactorial and include respiratory defects and cytosolic protestatic stress via mPOS.
source: The deleterious stressors downstream of clogging are likely to be multifactorial and include respiratory defects and cytosolic protestatic stress via mPOS.
evidence: This is inferred from the multiple phenotypes observed in the study.

claim: The IMM-associated AAA protease Yme1p (and not the proteasome) appears to be a major proteolytic pathway for clogged Aac2pA128P,A137D.
source: The IMM-associated AAA protease Yme1p (and not the proteasome) appears to be a major proteolytic pathway for clogged Aac2pA128P,A137D.
evidence: This is supported by the stabilization of the mutant protein in yme1Δ cells but not with proteasome inhibition.

claim: Genetic deletion of YME1 is well tolerated in yeast cells.
source: That genetic deletion of YME1 is well tolerated in yeast cells suggests that loss of Yme1-based proteolysis does not underlie toxicity of aac2A128P,A137D expression.
evidence: This is established knowledge about yme1Δ yeast.

claim: Clogging of the TOM complex is the primary mechanism of Aac2pA128P,A137D-induced protein import defects and the ensuing cell stress.
source: We propose that clogging of the TOM complex is the primary mechanism of Aac2pA128P,A137D-induced protein import defects and the ensuing cell stress.
evidence: This is the authors' proposed model based on their findings.

claim: In vitro experiments strongly support that Aac2pA128P,A137D is defective in translocating through the TOM complex in fully energized, wild-type mitochondria.
source: Importantly, the former is strongly supported by in vitro experiments showing that Aac2pA128P,A137D is defective in translocating through the TOM complex in fully energized, wild-type mitochondria.
evidence: This is based on the in vitro import assay data.

claim: The ADP/ATP carrier is one of the most abundant proteins in mitochondria, outnumbering the Tom40 pore-forming protein by almost an order of magnitude.
source: In the context of low Aac2pA128P,A137D levels in cells (just 4.7% of wild-type), it is important to note that the ADP/ATP carrier is one of the most abundant proteins in mitochondria, outnumbering the Tom40 pore-forming protein by almost an order of magnitude (Morgenstern et al., 2017; Pfanner et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge from published literature supported by citations.

claim: If ~70% of the reduced level of Aac2pA128P,A137D is actively clogging TOM complexes, this would still occupy ~30% of the Tom40 channels.
source: Thus, if ~70% of the reduced level of Aac2pA128P,A137D is actively clogging TOM complexes, this would still occupy ~30% of the Tom40 channels, which may have a considerable effect on general protein import.
evidence: This is a calculation based on protein abundance and clogging data.

claim: Occupying ~30% of Tom40 channels may have a considerable effect on general protein import.
source: Thus, if ~70% of the reduced level of Aac2pA128P,A137D is actively clogging TOM complexes, this would still occupy ~30% of the Tom40 channels, which may have a considerable effect on general protein import.

claim: The central importance of proper TOM complex function to mitochondrial and cell homeostasis provides physiological justification for the existence of multiple pathways dedicated to unclogging the TOM complex.
source: This reflects the central importance of proper TOM complex function to mitochondrial and cell homeostasis, and also provides physiological justification for the existence of multiple pathways dedicated to unclogging the TOM complex (Weidberg and Amon, 2018; Mårtensson et al., 2019).
evidence: This is inferred from the findings and supported by citations to published literature.

claim: A long-standing mystery in the mitochondrial disease field is how dominant mutations in SLC25A4 cause such a wide spectrum of clinical and molecular phenotypes that are not observed in patients with homozygous null SLC25A4.
source: A long-standing mystery in the mitochondrial disease field is how dominant mutations in SLC25A4 (encoding adenine nucleotide translocase 1 [Ant1]) cause such a wide spectrum of clinical and molecular phenotypes that are not observed in patients with homozygous null SLC25A4 (Kaukonen et al., 2000; Siciliano et al., 2003; Simoncini et al., 2017; Palmieri et al., 2005; Napoli et al., 2001; Deschauer et al., 2005; Thompson et al., 2016; Echaniz-Laguna et al., 2012; Tosserams et al., 2018; Kashiki et al., 2022).
evidence: This is established knowledge from published literature supported by multiple citations.

claim: The dominant pathogenic ANT1 proteins must have an unknown gain-of-function pathogenic mechanism.
source: The implication is that the dominant pathogenic ANT1 proteins must have an unknown gain-of-function pathogenic mechanism.
evidence: This is inferred from the difference in phenotypes between dominant mutations and null mutations.

claim: The phenotypes observed in Slc25a4 p.A114P,A123D/+ mice cannot be explained by haploinsufficiency or a dominant negative effect on ADP/ATP transport.

claim: The neurological and muscle phenotypes in Slc25a4 p.A114P,A123D/+ mice have never been reported in heterozygous Slc25a4 knockout mice despite 25 years of characterization.
source: First, as in humans, the neurological and muscle phenotypes in Slc25a4 p.A114P,A123D/+ mice have never been reported in heterozygous Slc25a4 knockout mice despite 25 years of characterization by Doug Wallace and colleagues.
evidence: This is based on the published literature on Slc25a4 knockout mice.

source: Second, mitochondria from Slc25a4 p.A114P,A123D/+ mouse muscle are able to exceed the maximal respiration rate of wild-type mitochondria when complex II is stimulated (Figure 6B), indicating that one functional copy of Ant1 is sufficient to support high respiratory rates without compensatory increase in other Ant isoforms (see Figure 8—figure supplement 1F; Figure 8—figure supplement 1—source data 1; Figure 8—figure supplement 2—source data 1; Figure 8—figure supplement 2F).

source: Second, mitochondria from Slc25a4 p.A114P,A123D/+ mouse muscle are able to exceed the maximal respiration rate of wild-type mitochondria when complex II is stimulated (Figure 6B), indicating that one functional copy of Ant1 is sufficient to support high respiratory rates without compensatory increase in other Ant isoforms (see Figure 8—figure supplement 1F; Figure 8—figure supplement 1—source data 1; Figure 8—figure supplement 2—source data 1; Figure 8—figure supplement 2F).

claim: The transcriptional profile in Slc25a4 p.A114P,A123D/+ skeletal muscle is entirely distinct from that in Slc25a4 knockout mice.
source: Third, the transcriptional profile in Slc25a4 p.A114P,A123D/+ skeletal muscle is entirely distinct from that in Slc25a4 knockout mice, suggesting different underlying mechanisms of muscle dysfunction (Morrow et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on comparative analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: Ant1 likely functions as a monomer.
source: Fourth, Ant1 likely functions as a monomer, making a dominant-negative mechanism of adenine nucleotide transport unlikely (Pebay-Peyroula et al., 2003; Ruprecht et al., 2019; Kunji and Ruprecht, 2020).

claim: A dominant-negative mechanism of adenine nucleotide transport by mutant Ant1 is unlikely.
source: Fourth, Ant1 likely functions as a monomer, making a dominant-negative mechanism of adenine nucleotide transport unlikely (Pebay-Peyroula et al., 2003; Ruprecht et al., 2019; Kunji and Ruprecht, 2020).

source: Finally, the yeast equivalent of Ant1A114P,A123D, Aac2pA128P,A137D, is catalytically inactive yet clearly exerts toxicity even in conditions where aac2Δ cells are healthy (Figure 1C).
